title: "Day 13 — Summarising groups without hiding the plants"

[Lecture slides](../lectures/13-group-summaries/lec.qmd) · [Quiz](13-group-summaries-quiz.qmd) · [Weekly revision](quiz.qmd)

## Today's question

A bar chart of two group means cannot tell a reader how many plants are behind
each bar, how much they varied, or whether one unusual plant pulled a mean up.
Today you make a small table with one row per group and a figure that shows
every plant together with its group mean, so a reader gets both.

Start `day13-groups.R` in the project root:

```{r}
library(readr)
library(dplyr)
library(ggplot2)
seedlings <- read_csv("data/seedlings.csv", show_col_types = FALSE) |>
  mutate(growth_mm = final_mm - initial_mm)
```

**Save today:** `day13-groups.R`, `output/growth-summary.csv` and
`output/growth-summary.png`.

## One row per group

Use `group_by()` and `summarise()` to find out the number of plants, mean,
median and SD of growth in each treatment group:

```{r}
group_summary <- seedlings |>
  group_by(treatment) |>
  summarise(n_plants = n(),
            n_observed = sum(!is.na(growth_mm)),
            mean_mm = mean(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            median_mm = median(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            sd_mm = sd(growth_mm, na.rm = TRUE),
            .groups = "drop")
group_summary
```

`group_by(treatment)` makes the next step work separately within each treatment,
and `summarise()` returns one row per group. The names left of `=` become the
column names. `n()` counts rows, that is plant records, while
`sum(!is.na(growth_mm))` counts the growth values that are actually there (`!`
means "not"). `.groups = "drop"` returns an ordinary table.

| treatment | n_plants | n_observed | mean_mm | median_mm | sd_mm |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| control | 12 | 12 | 15.28 | 15.65 | 3.19 |
| treated | 12 | 12 | 21.49 | 20.85 | 4.87 |

`group_summary` has two rows that describe groups; `seedlings` still has the 24
plants. You need both: the plants for the figure, the summary for the means.

## Plants and means in one figure

```{r}
group_plot <- ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = treatment, y = growth_mm)) +
  geom_point(position = position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0, seed = 13),
             alpha = 0.75) +
  geom_point(data = group_summary, aes(x = treatment, y = mean_mm),
             inherit.aes = FALSE, shape = 18, size = 4, colour = "darkred") +
  labs(x = "Treatment", y = "Change in seedling length (mm)",
       caption = "Small dots: individual plants. Red diamonds: group means.") +
  theme_minimal()
group_plot
```

The first `geom_point()` draws one dot per plant from `seedlings`.
`position_jitter(width = 0.08, height = 0)` moves dots a little sideways so they
do not hide each other, but never up or down, so every dot stays at its measured
growth. The second `geom_point()` takes its data from `group_summary` and draws
the means as red diamonds; `inherit.aes = FALSE` tells it to use its own `x` and
`y` instead of looking for `growth_mm`, which the summary table does not have.

The figure shows what the table cannot: the groups overlap, one treated plant grew
only 12.2 mm, and two treated plants grew about 30 mm. If you add whiskers, say
what they show. Mean ± SD describes how plants vary; a confidence interval, which
comes in week 4, describes how uncertain a mean is. Points and means without
whiskers are a good choice for today.

## Histograms

A **histogram** cuts the growth axis into intervals, called bins, and counts the
plants in each. Use one to find out the shape of each group's growth values:

```{r}
ggplot(seedlings, aes(x = growth_mm)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 4, boundary = 0, colour = "white") +
  facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1) +
  labs(x = "Change in seedling length (mm)", y = "Number of plants") +
  theme_minimal()
```

`facet_wrap(~ treatment, ncol = 1)` draws one panel per group, stacked on the same
growth axis so the panels can be compared. With 4 mm bins, most control plants
fall between 12 and 20 mm, and most treated plants between 20 and 24 mm, with two
treated plants in the 28–32 mm bin. With only 12 plants per group the shape
changes noticeably when you change the bin width.

## Saving the table and the figure

```{r}
write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv")
ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4)
```

The CSV holds the numbers and the PNG holds the picture; until you save them,
both exist only in R's memory. Find the two files in your file manager and open
them outside RStudio.

## Group summaries for the seedlings

1. Use `filter()` and `mean()` to find out whether the control mean in
   `group_summary` matches the plants it came from. You should get 15.28 mm.
2. Use the same summary code on `output/seedlings-cleaned.csv` from day 11 (add
   `growth_mm` if it is not there) to find out how the missing P06 shows up. Control
   has `n_plants` 12 but `n_observed` 11, and a mean of 15.21 mm instead of
   15.28 mm, because a different set of plants contributed. This is why the table
   keeps both counts.
3. Change the histogram's `binwidth` to 2 and then to 6 and find out which
   features stay the same. At every width the treated values sit higher than the
   controls and the two treated plants near 30 mm stand apart; smaller peaks and
   gaps appear or vanish with the bin width, so do not describe them.
4. Write a caption for `output/growth-summary.png` that a reader could check
   without the code: the unit (one plant), the outcome and its unit, what dots and
   diamonds mean, and n. For example: "Seven-day growth (mm) of 24 individually
   potted seedlings, 12 per group. Dots are plants; red diamonds are group means."

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true"}
## Hint: keep the two tables apart

`write_csv(group_summary, "output/growth-summary.csv")` saves the summary, while
`ggsave("output/growth-summary.png", plot = group_plot, width = 6, height = 4)`
saves the plot. If a layer complains about a column it cannot find, use `names()`
on the table that layer uses.
:::

## Another lab: percentage yield

Your teacher may choose this instead of task 2 above. In
`data/organic-recovery.csv` each row is one independent synthesis run. Calculate
`yield_percent = 100 * isolated_mass_g / theoretical_mass_g`, as on day 12, then
use `group_by(protocol)` and `summarise()` to find out the number of runs, mean
yield and SD for each protocol. Both protocols have six runs; the standard mean is
68.67% (SD 4.32 percentage points) and the modified mean 77.00% (SD 3.74).
Plot the runs with a mean marker as above, with the y-axis labelled
"Isolated product yield (%)", and save `output/organic-yield-summary.csv` and
`output/organic-yield-summary.png`.

## A second class's data

Make the same table and figure for `data/seedlings-transfer.csv` (18 plants, nine
per group) in a new script, `day13-transfer.R`, with its own `library()` lines,
import and growth calculation.

1. Use `group_by()` and `summarise()` to make `transfer_summary` with n, mean,
   median and SD, and save it as `output/day13-transfer-summary.csv`. Use
   `nrow()` to find out how many rows `transfer` and `transfer_summary` have: 18
   plants and 2 groups. You should get means of 13.66 mm (control) and 17.87 mm
   (treated).
2. Draw the plants with a mean marker from `transfer_summary`, with a caption that
   says n = 9 per group, and save it as `output/day13-transfer-points.png`. Does
   any control plant grow more than a treated plant? Yes: three control plants
   (15.9, 16.3 and 17.4 mm) grew more than the smallest treated plant (15.0 mm).
3. Restart R and rerun the script to find out whether it rebuilds both files on
   its own.

## Check your understanding

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Why show individual dots as well as the means?

The dots show how many plants there are, how much they vary, where unusual
values lie and how much the groups overlap. A higher mean does not mean every
treated plant grew more than every control plant.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## The summary table has two rows. Are they two new observations?

No. Each row describes a group of 12 plants. The 24 plants stay in `seedlings`,
and that is the table any later analysis uses.
:::

**Keep:** `day13-groups.R`, `output/growth-summary.csv`,
`output/growth-summary.png` and your caption.
